If $\xi$~is itself a positive integer, we can take $\delta$ to be any number less than~$1$, and (i)~will be true; or, if $\xi$~is halfway between two positive integers, we can take $\delta$ to be any number less than~$\frac{1}{2}$. excerpts.markdown: Suppose, for example, that $S$ consists of the points corresponding to all the positive integers. If $\xi$ is itself a positive integer, we can take $\delta$ to be any number less than $1$, and (i) will be true; or, if $\xi$ is halfway between two positive integers, we can take $\delta$ to be any number less than $\frac{1}{2}$. On the other hand, if $S$ consists of all the rational points, then, whatever the value of $\xi$, (ii) is true; for any interval whatever contains an infinity of rational points.
excerpts.why: Contrasts a set with no accumulation points (the integers) with one where every point is one (the rationals).

excerpts.location: REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.location: REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.markdown: Two pure quadratic surds are said to be *similar* if they can be expressed as rational multiples of the same surd, and otherwise to be *dissimilar*.
excerpts.why: It gives a clear test for when two surds can be combined and compared, which is the basis for simplifying surd sums.

excerpts.why: It shows why the two-class description must cover every real number, since √2 otherwise escapes classification.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.markdown: It is known that a much better approximation to the true relation can then be found by means of what is known as ‘van der Waals’ law’, expressed by the equation

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: In these circumstances $y$~is said to be a \emph{function} of~$x$. This notion of functional dependence of one variable upon another is perhaps the most important in the whole range of higher mathematics.

excerpts.why: States the central definition and tells the learner why it deserves care.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: All that is essential is that there should be some relation between $x$~and~$y$ such that to some values of~$x$ at any rate correspond values of~$y$.
excerpts.markdown: All that is essential is that there should be some relation between $x$ and $y$ such that to some values of $x$ at any rate correspond values of $y$.
excerpts.why: Frees the learner from the false belief that a function must have a formula and be defined everywhere.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.markdown: Boyle’s law, however, only gives a reasonable approximation to the facts provided the gas is not compressed too much. When $v$ is decreased and $p$ increased beyond a certain point, the relation between them is no longer expressed with tolerable exactness by the equation (i).
excerpts.why: Shows that a physical law is an approximation with limits, and that a function may be defined by different formulas on different ranges.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: Let $y$~be defined as \emph{the height in inches of policeman~$Cx$, in the Metropolitan Police, at {\upshape5.30}~\DPchg{p.m.}{\textsc{p.m.}}\ on {\upshape8}~Aug.~{\upshape1907}}. Then $y$~is defined for a certain number of integral values of~$x$, viz.\ $1$, $2$, \dots,~$N$, where $N$~is the total number of policemen in division~$C$ at that particular moment of time.
excerpts.markdown: Let $y$ be defined as *the height in inches of policeman $Cx$, in the Metropolitan Police, at 5.30 p.m.p.m. on 8 Aug. 1907*. excerpts.why: A vivid, charming example of a function with no formula that is defined only for a finite set of whole numbers.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: The reader has no doubt some notion as to what is meant by a \emph{continuous} curve, a curve without breaks or jumps; such a curve, in fact, as is roughly represented in \Fig{8}.
excerpts.markdown: The reader has no doubt some notion as to what is meant by a *continuous* curve, a curve without breaks or jumps; such a curve, in fact, as is roughly represented in [fig:8]Fig. 8.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: Consider for example the function~$x/x$, which is a rational function. On removing the common factor~$x$ we obtain $1/1 = 1$. But the original function is not \emph{always} equal to~$1$: it is equal to~$1$ only so long as $x\neq 0$. If $x = 0$ it takes the form~$0/0$, which is meaningless.
excerpts.markdown: Consider for example the function $x/x$, which is a rational function. On removing the common factor $x$ we obtain $1/1 = 1$. But the original function is not *always* equal to $1$: it is equal to $1$ only so long as $x\neq 0$. If $x = 0$ it takes the form $0/0$, which is meaningless.
excerpts.why: Warns of a common mistake: cancelling a common factor can change a function at exceptional values.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: It is in no way presupposed in the definition of a rational function that the constants which occur as coefficients should be rational \emph{numbers}. The word rational has reference solely to the way in which the variable~$x$ appears in the function.
excerpts.markdown: It is in no way presupposed in the definition of a rational function that the constants which occur as coefficients should be rational *numbers*. The word rational has reference solely to the way in which the variable $x$ appears in the function.
excerpts.why: Clears up a likely confusion between a rational function and rational numbers.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: We can in this case at once obtain a direct relation between $x$~and~$y$ by squaring and adding: we find that $x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$, $t$~being now eliminated.
excerpts.markdown: We can in this case at once obtain a direct relation between $x$ and $y$ by squaring and adding: we find that $x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$, $t$ being now eliminated.
excerpts.why: It shows how eliminating the auxiliary variable turns a parametric curve back into a familiar equation.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: Starting from a unit length we can construct any \emph{rational} length.
excerpts.markdown: Starting from a unit length we can construct any *rational* length.
excerpts.why: Shows that rational lengths are the starting point of every ruler construction, a useful anchor for the idea of constructible numbers.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: Show that if $x$~is a rational function of~$y$, and $y$~is a rational function of~$x$, then $Axy + Bx + Cy + D = 0$.
excerpts.markdown: Show that if $x$ is a rational function of $y$, and $y$ is a rational function of $x$, then $Axy + Bx + Cy + D = 0$.
excerpts.why: A short proof exercise that shows how two functional relations force a symmetric linear form.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
If $f(x) = f(-x)$ for all values of~$x$, $f(x)$~is called an \emph{even} function.
If $f(x) = -f(-x)$, it is called an \emph{odd} function.
excerpts.markdown: If $f(x) = f(-x)$ for all values of $x$, $f(x)$ is called an *even* function. If $f(x) = -f(-x)$, it is called an *odd* function.
excerpts.why: Gives the two symmetric definitions side by side, ready for the exercise showing every function splits into even and odd parts.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
All these constructions
were what may be called Euclidean constructions; they depended
on the ruler and compasses only.
excerpts.markdown: All these constructions were what may be called Euclidean constructions; they depended on the ruler and compasses only.
excerpts.why: Names the ruler-and-compasses rules that frame everything the exercise then proves about constructible lengths.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
This expression contains a fourth root, but this is of
course the square root of a square root.
excerpts.markdown: This expression contains a fourth root, but this is of course the square root of a square root.
excerpts.why: Shows a learner that a daunting nested radical is only repeated square roots, hence constructible.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
Conversely, \emph{only} irrationals of this kind can be constructed by Euclidean
methods. Starting from a unit length we can construct any \emph{rational} length.
excerpts.markdown: Conversely, *only* irrationals of this kind can be constructed by Euclidean methods. Starting from a unit length we can construct any *rational* length.
excerpts.why: States the converse half of the result and the starting point of the argument: what is constructible is limited, and rational lengths are the base.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
Hence \emph{Euclidean methods will construct any surd expression involving square
roots only, and no others}.
excerpts.markdown: Hence *Euclidean methods will construct any surd expression involving square roots only, and no others*.
excerpts.why: The exercise's central conclusion, a clean statement of exactly what ruler and compasses can do.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
One of the famous problems of antiquity was that of the duplication of
the cube, that is to say of the construction by Euclidean methods of a
length measured by~$\sqrt[3]{2}$. It can be shown that $\sqrt[3]{2}$~cannot be expressed by
means of any finite combination of rational numbers and square roots, and so
that the problem is an impossible one.
excerpts.markdown: One of the famous problems of antiquity was that of the duplication of the cube, that is to say of the construction by Euclidean methods of a length measured by $\sqrt[3]{2}$. It can be shown that $\sqrt[3]{2}$ cannot be expressed by means of any finite combination of rational numbers and square roots, and so that the problem is an impossible one.
excerpts.why: Connects an ancient problem to the constructibility result, showing how a proof of impossibility works.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex:
If $R$~is the earth's
radius, the error in supposing $AM$ to be its circumference is less than $11$~yards.
excerpts.markdown: If $R$ is the earth’s radius, the error in supposing $AM$ to be its circumference is less than $11$ yards.
excerpts.why: Makes the accuracy of an approximate construction vivid by scaling it to the size of the earth.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.markdown: It will at once suggest a contoured Ordnance Survey map: and in fact this is the principle on which such maps are constructed.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.markdown: *a function $y = f(x)$ will be said to be an algebraical function of $x$ if it is the root of an equation such as (1), *i.e.* the root of an equation of the $m$th degree in $y$, whose coefficients are rational functions of $x$*.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner the single definition the whole section turns on: an algebraic function is any root of a polynomial equation whose coefficients are rational in x.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: A function is said to be \emph{periodic}, with period~$a$, if $f(x) = f(x + a)$ for all values of~$x$ for which $f(x)$~is defined.
excerpts.markdown: A function is said to be *periodic*, with period $a$, if $f(x) = f(x + a)$ for all values of $x$ for which $f(x)$ is defined.
excerpts.why: It states the definition of a period precisely, so a learner can test any function against it.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: The locus is the surface formed by drawing lines parallel to~$OZ$ through all points of this curve. Such a surface is called a \emph{cylinder}.
excerpts.markdown: The locus is the surface formed by drawing lines parallel to $OZ$ through all points of this curve. Such a surface is called a *cylinder*.
excerpts.why: It shows how a cylinder is built from a plane curve, which makes the three-dimensional figure easy to picture.

excerpts.latex: It is entirely built up of straight lines; but the surface is curved everywhere, and is in general shape not unlike certain forms of table-napkin rings (\Fig{18c}).
excerpts.markdown: It is entirely built up of straight lines; but the surface is curved everywhere, and is in general shape not unlike certain forms of table-napkin rings ([fig:18c]Fig. 18c).

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES

excerpts.markdown: The abscissae of its intersections with the axis of $x$ are the roots of the equation.

excerpts.markdown: This function is defined for all values of $x$ for which $R_{1}^{2} \geq 4R_{2}$.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: We are therefore led to give the following definition: \emph{a function $y = f(x)$ will be said to be an algebraical function of~$x$ if it is the root of an equation such as~\Eq{(1)}, \ie~the root of an equation of the $m$\textsuperscript{th}~degree in~$y$, whose coefficients are rational functions of~$x$}.
excerpts.markdown: We are therefore led to give the following definition: *a function $y = f(x)$ will be said to be an algebraical function of $x$ if it is the root of an equation such as (1), *i.e.* the root of an equation of the $m$th degree in $y$, whose coefficients are rational functions of $x$*.

excerpts.latex: For it is known that in general such an equation as~\Eq{(1)} cannot be solved explicitly for~$y$ in terms of~$x$, when $m$~is greater than~$4$, though such a solution is always possible if $m = 1$, $2$,~$3$, or~$4$ and in special cases for higher values of~$m$.
excerpts.markdown: For it is known that in general such an equation as (1) cannot be solved explicitly for $y$ in terms of $x$, when $m$ is greater than $4$, though such a solution is always possible if $m = 1$, $2$, $3$, or $4$ and in special cases for higher values of $m$.
excerpts.why: It shows why implicit algebraical functions are a real extension of the explicit ones, and where explicit solution breaks down.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: All functions of~$x$ which are not rational or even algebraical are called \emph{transcendental} functions. This class of functions, being defined in so purely negative a manner, naturally includes an infinite variety of whole kinds of functions of varying degrees of simplicity and importance.
excerpts.markdown: All functions of $x$ which are not rational or even algebraical are called *transcendental* functions. This class of functions, being defined in so purely negative a manner, naturally includes an infinite variety of whole kinds of functions of varying degrees of simplicity and importance.
excerpts.why: It names the class and honestly notes that a purely negative definition gathers very different kinds of function together.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: It is easy to see that no periodic function can be a rational function, unless it is a constant.
excerpts.markdown: It is easy to see that no periodic function can be a rational function, unless it is a constant.
excerpts.why: It states the key fact behind the proof that cos x and sin x are not rational.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: It oscillates up and down, the rapidity of the oscillations becoming greater and greater as $x$~approaches~$0$. For $x = 0$ the function is undefined.
excerpts.markdown: It oscillates up and down, the rapidity of the oscillations becoming greater and greater as $x$ approaches $0$. For $x = 0$ the function is undefined.
excerpts.why: It describes the graph of sin(1/x) vividly and shows a function that is perfectly well behaved yet undefined at a point.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: The function~$y$ does in point of fact answer to the definition of a function: there is a relation between $x$~and~$y$ such that when $x$~is known $y$~is known. We are perfectly at liberty to take this relation to be what we please, however arbitrary and apparently futile.
excerpts.markdown: The function $y$ does in point of fact answer to the definition of a function: there is a relation between $x$ and $y$ such that when $x$ is known $y$ is known. We are perfectly at liberty to take this relation to be what we please, however arbitrary and apparently futile.
excerpts.why: It tells learners that a function need not follow a single formula and answers the natural objection to a function that is odd at integers.

excerpts.location: FUNCTIONS OF REAL VARIABLES
excerpts.latex: A particle which moves along a straight line has only \emph{one degree of freedom}. Its direction of motion is fixed; its position can be completely fixed by one measurement of position, \eg\ by its distance from a fixed point on the line.
excerpts.markdown: A particle which moves along a straight line has only *one degree of freedom*. Its direction of motion is fixed; its position can be completely fixed by one measurement of position, *e.g.* by its distance from a fixed point on the line.
excerpts.why: It gives an intuitive physical meaning to the number of coordinates needed to fix a point on a line, in a plane, or in space.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS
excerpts.latex: \Fig{24} is usually known as Argand's diagram.
excerpts.markdown: [fig:24]Fig. 24 is usually known as Argand’s diagram.
excerpts.why: Tells the learner where the plane picture of complex numbers gets its name, which helps when the diagram is cited in other books.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS
excerpts.latex: When $y = 0$ we say that \emph{$z$~is real}, when $x = 0$ that \emph{$z$~is purely imaginary}.
excerpts.markdown: When $y = 0$ we say that *$z$ is real*, when $x = 0$ that *$z$ is purely imaginary*.
excerpts.why: Gives the two special cases of a complex number in one plain sentence, so the learner can see when the imaginary part vanishes.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS
excerpts.latex: Two numbers $x + yi$, $x - yi$ which differ only in the signs of their imaginary parts, we call \emph{conjugate}.
excerpts.markdown: Two numbers $x + yi$, $x - yi$ which differ only in the signs of their imaginary parts, we call *conjugate*.
excerpts.why: Defines conjugate complex numbers exactly, which the learner needs before rationalizing denominators or reading the theorem on roots.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS

excerpts.markdown: There are other special values of $n$ for which such constructions are possible, the most interesting being $n = 17$.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS

excerpts.markdown: Common sense at once suggests that we should define the sum of two displacements as the displacement which is the result of the successive application of the two given displacements.
excerpts.why: It shows the reasoning behind the definition of addition before any formula appears, so the learner sees why the rule is chosen.

excerpts.markdown: In other words, *addition of displacements obeys the commutative law* expressed in ordinary algebra by the equation $a + b = b + a$.

excerpts.markdown: The required definition is therefore [x, y] [x’, y’] = [xx’ - yy’, xy’ + yx’]. (6)

excerpts.markdown: The application of any of the ordinary algebraical operations to complex numbers will yield only complex numbers.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS

excerpts.markdown: One most important property of real numbers is that known as *the factor theorem*, which asserts that *the product of two numbers cannot be zero unless one of the two is itself zero*.
excerpts.why: It states the zero-product property that the chapter then extends to complex numbers.

excerpts.location: COMPLEX NUMBERS

excerpts.markdown: All such theorems as these are true whether $a$, $b$, … $\alpha$, $\beta$, … are real or complex.

excerpts.markdown: in this notation, suggested by Profs. Harkness and Morley, De Moivre’s theorem is expressed by the equation $(\Cis\theta)^{n} = \Cis n\theta$.
excerpts.why: A historical remark showing where the compact cis notation came from and how it makes De Moivre's theorem look simple.

excerpts.markdown: [The amplitudes have not necessarily their principal values.]

symbols.meaning: function of a positive integer variable

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The limit of a product of two sequences is the product of their limits.

symbols.meaning: function of a positive integer variable
second function of a positive integer variable

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: If the series u_1 + u_2 + u_3 + … converges, its terms u_n tend to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The modulus of a complex number φ(n) = ρ(n) + iσ(n) is the square root of the sum of the squares of its real and imaginary parts.

symbols.meaning: complex function of a positive integer variable

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The product of two complex numbers is split into real and imaginary parts.

symbols.meaning: complex function of n, equal to ρ(n) + iσ(n)
complex function of n, equal to ρ'(n) + iσ'(n)

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: A complex function φ(n) is written as its real part ρ(n) plus i times its imaginary part σ(n).

symbols.meaning: complex function of a positive integer variable

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The n-th power of a complex number in polar form has modulus r^n and angle nθ.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The modulus of z^n equals r^n, where r is the modulus of z.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: For complex z with modulus r < 1, z^n tends to zero as n tends to infinity.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: If z^n tends to a limit l, then l equals zl, which forces l = 0 unless z = 1.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A POSITIVE INTEGRAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The sum of the first n terms of the geometric series in z equals (1 - z^n)/(1 - z) when z is not 1.

symbols.meaning: sum of the first n terms of the geometric series

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For x at or beyond some x0(Delta), phi(x) differs from l by less than any chosen positive Delta, which is the condition for phi(x) to tend to l as x tends to infinity.

symbols.meaning: one-valued function of the continuous variable x
a positive number, however small, assigned in advance

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) tends to the limit l as x tends to infinity.

symbols.meaning: one-valued function of the continuous variable x

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) tends to -infinity with x, the mirror of the definition of tending to +infinity.

symbols.meaning: one-valued function of the continuous variable x

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Notation for phi(x) tending to +infinity, as in Definition 2.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(y) tends to the limit l as y tends to 0 through positive values.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(y) tends to the limit l as y tends to 0 from both sides, with y different from zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) tends to the limit l as x tends to a; the value at x = a itself plays no part.

symbols.meaning: function of the continuous variable x

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) tends to l as x approaches a from the right, through values greater than a.

symbols.meaning: function of the continuous variable x

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The right-hand limit of phi at a is written phi(a+0).

symbols.meaning: the limit of phi(x) as x tends to a from the right

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For a function that is steadily increasing near a, its left-hand limit at a is no greater than its value at a, which is no greater than its right-hand limit.

symbols.meaning: left-hand limit of phi at a
right-hand limit of phi at a

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: If phi(x) is identically zero, its limit as x tends to zero is zero.

symbols.meaning: the function defined as zero for all x

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: A function equal to phi(x) except that psi(0) = 1 still has limit zero at x = 0, since the limit ignores the value at 0.

symbols.meaning: function equal to zero except psi(0) = 1

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: psi(x) is the greatest integer not greater than 1 - x^2; it equals 1 at x = 0 and 0 for 0 < |x| < 1.

symbols.meaning: function defined by the greatest-integer bracket
the greatest integer not greater than the enclosed number

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The function x/x has limit 1 as x tends to zero, although it is not defined at x = 0.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For phi(x) = ((x+1)^2 - 1)/x, which equals x + 2 for x not zero, the limit as x tends to zero is 2.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For x not zero, phi(x) equals x + 2, so it is defined by the expression except at x = 0.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of sine x to x tends to 1 as x tends to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For x positive and less than pi/2, sine x is less than x, which is less than tangent x; this is the inequality used to prove the limit of sin x over x.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The quantity 1 minus cosine x, divided by x squared, tends to one half as x tends to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of the inverse sine of x to x tends to 1 as x tends to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of sin(alpha x) to x tends to alpha as x tends to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of tan(alpha x) to x tends to alpha as x tends to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The difference cosecant x minus cotangent x, divided by x, tends to one half as x tends to zero.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of 1 + cos(pi x) to tan^2(pi x) tends to one half as x tends to 1.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The difference quotient of x squared tends to 2a as x tends to a.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For any integer m, the difference quotient of x^m tends to m a^(m-1) as x tends to a.
equations.sympy: Eq(Limit((x**m - a**m)/(x - a), x, a), m*a**(m - 1))

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of the two polynomials tends to 1 as x tends to 1, since x - 1 is a factor of both.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For any integer m (except a = 0 with m negative), x^m tends to a^m as x tends to a.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: A rational function R tends to its value at a whenever a is not a root of its denominator.

symbols.meaning: point approached, not a root of the denominator

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: A polynomial in x tends to its constant term as x tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: positive integer, degree of the polynomial

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of two polynomials in x tends to a over alpha as x tends to zero, provided alpha is not zero.

symbols.meaning: constant leading coefficients of numerator and denominator

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The sum of two functions tending to limits l and l' tends to l + l'.

symbols.meaning: functions tending to limits as x tends to a

equations.sympy: Eq(Limit(phi(x) + psi(x), x, a), l + lp)

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The product of two functions tending to limits l and l' tends to ll'.

symbols.meaning: functions tending to limits as x tends to a

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The quotient of two functions tending to limits l and l' tends to l/l', unless l' is zero.

symbols.meaning: functions tending to limits as x tends to a
their respective limits, l' not zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: x^2 is of smaller order than x as x tends to zero, since x^2/x tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: continuous real variable tending to zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Dividing phi(x) by x^(-k) is the same as multiplying it by x^k; the order of greatness of phi when x is small is decided by this product tending to a nonzero limit.

symbols.meaning: function large when x is small
continuous real variable tending to zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The square root of 1 + x and the square root of 1 - x both tend to 1 as x tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: continuous real variable tending to zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The difference of the two square roots divided by x tends to 1 as x tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: continuous real variable tending to zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The square root of 1 + x + x^2, less 1, divided by x tends to one half as x tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: continuous real variable tending to zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) is bounded in an interval around a when it lies between two fixed constants H and K there.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) tends to l as x tends to a exactly when its lower and upper limits of indetermination both equal l.

symbols.meaning: lower limit of indetermination of phi(x) as x tends to a
upper limit of indetermination of phi(x) as x tends to a

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The principle of convergence: phi(x) tends to a limit as x tends to a exactly when values of phi at two points close to a differ by less than any given Delta.

symbols.meaning: two values of x close to a

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) is steadily increasing with x when its value at any larger x_2 is at least its value at any smaller x_1.

symbols.meaning: values of the continuous variable with x_2 > x_1

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: phi(x) is steadily increasing in the stricter sense when, for x_2 > x_1, its value at x_2 is strictly greater than at x_1.

symbols.meaning: values of the continuous variable with x_2 > x_1

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The value of the function at x stays within a given small amount DELTA of its value at xi; this is the fundamental inequality of continuity, which the book shows is equivalent to the limit definition.

symbols.meaning: the particular value of x at which continuity is tested
an arbitrarily small positive number bounding the difference of function values

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: A function is continuous at xi exactly when its left-hand limit, its value at xi, and its right-hand limit at xi are all equal.

symbols.meaning: the point at which continuity is tested
limit of phi as x approaches xi from values less than xi
limit of phi as x approaches xi from values greater than xi

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For continuity at x = a, the one-sided limits from below and above must both exist and equal the value phi(a).

symbols.meaning: the point of the variable at which continuity is examined
limit of phi as x approaches a from values less than a
limit of phi as x approaches a from values greater than a

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The function is bounded above when some fixed number K is never exceeded by any of its values in the interval.

symbols.meaning: a number bounding the function from above

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.latex: O(a, b) = M(a, b) - m(a, b)
equations.statement: The oscillation of a bounded function in an interval is the difference between its upper bound and its lower bound in that interval.

symbols.meaning: oscillation of the function in the interval (a, b)
upper bound of the function in the interval (a, b)
lower bound of the function in the interval (a, b)

equations.sympy: Eq(O(a, b), M(a, b) - m(a, b))

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.latex: O(a, b) \leq O(a, c) + O(c, b)
equations.statement: The oscillation over the whole interval from a to b is at most the sum of the oscillations over the two parts a to c and c to b.

symbols.meaning: oscillation of the function in the interval (a, b)
a point between a and b dividing the interval

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The standard rational function R(x) is the quotient of two polynomials P(x) and Q(x).

symbols.meaning: the standard rational function of x

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The difference between sin of x plus h and sin of x equals twice sin of half h times cos of x plus half h, which shows sin x is continuous.

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The function phi(x, y) is continuous at (xi, eta) when every value within a small enough square around that point differs from phi(xi, eta) by less than any given positive Delta.

symbols.meaning: function of the two variables x and y
the point (xi, eta) at which continuity is tested
an arbitrary positive number, however small

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Example function of two variables, defined as 2xy/(x^2+y^2) away from the axes and 0 when x or y is zero, which is continuous in each variable separately but not jointly at (0, 0).

symbols.meaning: the example function of two variables

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Along the straight line y = ax, the example function tends to 2a/(1+a^2), which depends on a, so the joint limit at (0, 0) does not exist.

symbols.meaning: the example function of two variables
slope of the line y = ax along which x and y tend to zero

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The relation between x and y that defines y as an implicit function of x, which by the theorem has a unique continuous solution vanishing with x.

symbols.meaning: implicit function of x defined by the relation

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For f(x, y) = y^5 - xy - y - x, the difference f(x, y) - f(x, y') factors as (y - y') times a second factor, which is the basis for checking that f is steadily decreasing in y.

symbols.meaning: the left-hand function y^5 - xy - y - x of the implicit equation
a second value of the variable y

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Solution of the quadratic y^2 - xy - y - x = 0 as an explicit function of x, using the positive square root.

symbols.meaning: implicit function of x given by the quadratic

equations.location: LIMITS OF FUNCTIONS OF A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Because f{x, phi(x)} = 0 and f is continuous, the value of f at the limit point (a, lambda) is zero, which forces lambda = b.

symbols.meaning: the continuous function of x and y in the neighbourhood of (a, b)
the x-value at which continuity of the implicit function is tested
limit of indetermination (inferior limit) of phi(x) as x tends to a

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The limit of the difference quotient of phi at x, as h tends to zero, equals the tangent of the angle psi that the tangent at P makes with OX.

symbols.meaning: function whose graph is the curve
abscissa of the fixed point P on the curve
increment of x (signed; Q has abscissa x + h)
angle the tangent PT makes with OX

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of phi at x is defined as the limit of the difference quotient as h tends to zero, without any geometrical picture.

symbols.meaning: derivative (differential coefficient) of phi at x

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: A polynomial of degree n in x written as a sum of powers of x with constant coefficients.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a polynomial of degree n is obtained by multiplying each term's coefficient by its power and lowering that power by one.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a polynomial written in binomial form, with binomial coefficients, is n times a polynomial of degree n-1 of the same binomial type.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: A polynomial of degree n factorises into n linear factors, with real or complex roots alpha.

symbols.meaning: roots of phi(x) = 0, real or complex

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a factored polynomial is a_0 times the sum of all products of n-1 of its linear factors.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a polynomial with repeated roots, each factor raised to multiplicity m, is a sum over the roots with the multiplicity lowering by one for the differentiated factor.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a quotient of two polynomials equals (P'Q - PQ') divided by Q squared.

symbols.meaning: derivatives of the polynomials P and Q

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of the partial-fraction term A over (x - alpha) to the power p is -pA over (x - alpha) to the power p+1.

symbols.meaning: constant numerator of the partial fraction term

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a sum of two differentiable functions is the sum of their derivatives.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a constant multiple of a function is the constant times the derivative of the function.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a product of two differentiable functions is f times F-prime plus f-prime times F.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of the reciprocal of a function is minus its derivative divided by the square of the function, where f is non-zero.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a quotient f over F is (f'F - fF') divided by F squared.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of a composite function F of f(x) is F-prime evaluated at f(x), times f-prime(x) (chain rule).

symbols.meaning: derivative of F evaluated at f(x)

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of the inverse function phi is the reciprocal of the derivative of psi, evaluated at y = phi(x).

symbols.meaning: continuous strictly monotone function with x = psi(y)

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: In differential notation, the derivative of a sum y = y1 + y2 is the sum of the derivatives.

symbols.meaning: dependent variables that are functions of x

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: In differential notation, the derivative of k times y1 is k times the derivative of y1.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: In differential notation, the derivative of a product y = y1 y2 is y1 times dy2/dx plus y2 times dy1/dx.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: In differential notation, the derivative of 1/y1 is minus dy1/dx divided by y1 squared.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: In differential notation, the derivative of the quotient y1/y2 is (y2 dy1/dx - y1 dy2/dx) divided by y2 squared.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: In differential notation, the chain rule: dz/dx equals dz/dy times dy/dx when z is a function of y and y of x.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of y with respect to x is the reciprocal of the derivative of x with respect to y, for an inverse function.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.name: equation of the tangent
equations.statement: The tangent to the curve y = phi(x) at (x0, y0) is the line through that point with slope phi'(x0).

symbols.meaning: point of contact on the curve
derivative at x0, the slope of the tangent

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.name: equation of the normal
equations.statement: The normal at (x0, y0) is the line through that point perpendicular to the tangent.

symbols.meaning: point of contact on the curve
derivative at x0, slope of the tangent

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: For y = x^m with m = p/q, the derivative with respect to x is mx^(m-1), obtained through the substitution z = x^(1/q) and the chain rule.

symbols.meaning: x^(1/q), so that x = z^q and y = z^p

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of phi(x) is the limit of the difference quotient as h tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: increment of x tending to zero

equations.sympy: Eq(Derivative(phi(x), x), limit(((x + h)**m - x**m)/h, h, 0))

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The limit of the difference quotient taken with xi tending to x gives the derivative mx^(m-1) of x^m.
equations.sympy: Eq(limit((xi**m - x**m)/(xi - x), xi, x), m*x**(m - 1))

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of (ax + b) raised to the power m is ma(ax + b)^(m-1), valid for all rational m.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The implicit relation between x and y used as the example for differentiating an implicit algebraic function.

symbols.meaning: dependent variable defined implicitly by the equation

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The result of differentiating x^3 + y^3 - 3axy = 0 with respect to x, which contains dy/dx.
equations.sympy: Eq(x**2 + y**2*Derivative(y, x) - a*(y + x*Derivative(y, x)), 0)

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of the implicitly defined y with respect to x, found by solving the differentiated equation.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of sin x with respect to x is cos x.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of cos x with respect to x is minus sin x.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of tan x is sec^2 x.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS
equations.statement: The derivative of cot x is minus cosec^2 x.

equations.location: DERIVATIVES AND INTEGRALS

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.name: exponential series
equations.statement: e^x equals the infinite power series 1 + x + x²/2! + … ; this is the exponential series.

symbols.meaning: a non-negative integer index of the terms

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: Euler's number e is the sum of the series 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + …

symbols.meaning: the number whose logarithm is 1 (Euler's number)
a non-negative integer index of the terms

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.name: exponential theorem
equations.statement: The x-th power of the series for e equals the exponential series in x.

symbols.meaning: a non-negative integer index of the terms

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: a^x equals e^(x log a), and so equals the exponential series in x log a, for positive a.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: For x > 0 and n > x, the partial sum E_n(x) of the exponential series lies between (1 + x/n)^n and (1 − x/n)^(−n).

symbols.meaning: the partial sum 1 + x + x²/2! + … + x^n/n!
a positive integer greater than x

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The exponential series satisfies the functional equation f(x)f(y) = f(x+y).

symbols.meaning: the exponential series as a function of x

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: Since f(x)f(y) = f(x+y), f(x) times f(−x) equals f(0), which is 1.

symbols.meaning: the exponential series as a function of x

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: log(1 + x) is the definite integral of 1/(1 + t) from 0 to x.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: 1/(1 + t) equals the first m terms of the geometric-type series 1 − t + t² − … plus a remainder term.

symbols.meaning: a positive integer number of terms

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The remainder R_m is the integral of t^m/(1 + t) from 0 to x.

symbols.meaning: the remainder after m terms of the logarithmic series

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: For negative x, with x = −ξ and t = −u, the remainder R_m equals (−1)^m times an integral with positive integrand.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The absolute value of R_m is positive and bounded by the integral of u^m scaled by 1/(1 − ξ), which tends to zero.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.name: logarithmic series
equations.statement: log(1 + x) equals x − x²/2 + x³/3 − … for −1 < x ≤ 1.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − … sums to log 2, the case x = 1 of the logarithmic series.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The inverse tangent of x is the integral of dt/(1 + t^2) from 0 to x.

symbols.meaning: real variable, upper limit of the integral

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: Setting x = 1 in the arctangent series gives pi/4 as the alternating series 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ...

symbols.meaning: the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The inverse hyperbolic tangent of x equals half the logarithm of (1 + x)/(1 - x).

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: For irrational m, (1 + x)^m is written as e to the power m log(1 + x).

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The derivative of (1 + x)^m with respect to x is m(1 + x)^(m-1), so the differentiation rule is unchanged for irrational m.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The function exp x is defined as the sum of the exponential series.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The exponential of a sum is the product of the exponentials.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The derivative of exp x with respect to x is exp x itself.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: With y = exp x, the derivative dy/dx equals y.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The logarithm of y is the integral of dt/t from 1 to y, so x is the logarithm of y.

symbols.meaning: positive real number, upper limit (equal to exp x)

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: For a positive integer n, the n-th power of exp x equals exp(nx).

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: The product of exp x and exp(-x) is 1, which extends the result to negative values.

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: exp x is the same as e raised to the power x, where e is exp 1.

symbols.meaning: real variable (rational here, extended to all real x)

equations.location: THE LOGARITHMIC AND EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS \\ OF A REAL VARIABLE
equations.statement: Euler's number e is exp 1, given by the sum of the exponential series at x = 1.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The complex variable z is written as x plus i times y, with x and y real.

symbols.meaning: coefficient of i in z (imaginary part)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: modulus
equations.statement: The modulus of z is the square root of x squared plus y squared.

symbols.meaning: imaginary part of z (coefficient of i)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The amplitude of z is the arctangent of y over x.

symbols.meaning: amplitude of the complex variable z

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: curvilinear integral
equations.statement: The real curvilinear integral of g dx + h dy along the path C is defined as the ordinary integral obtained by substituting the parametric equations of C.

symbols.meaning: path of integration (arc of a curve from A to B)
continuous function of x and y
continuous function of x and y
coordinate of a point on C
coordinate of a point on C

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: complex curvilinear integral
equations.statement: The integral of f(z) dz along C is defined as the real curvilinear integrals of (u dx - v dy) plus i times those of (v dx + u dy), where f = u + iv.

symbols.meaning: path of integration in Argand's diagram
polynomial or rational function of z

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: general logarithm
equations.statement: The general logarithm of zeta is the integral of dz/z along any curve C from 1 to zeta that does not pass through the origin.

symbols.meaning: path of integration from 1 to zeta avoiding the origin

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: A complex number zeta is written in polar form with modulus rho and amplitude phi.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: principal value of the logarithm
equations.statement: When the path of integration is a straight line from 1 to zeta, the value of Log zeta is log rho plus i phi.

symbols.meaning: general logarithm of zeta (here its principal value)
amplitude of zeta, between -pi and pi

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: principal value of the logarithm
equations.statement: The principal value of Log zeta, written log zeta, equals log rho plus i phi, with imaginary part between -pi and pi.

symbols.meaning: principal value of the general logarithm of zeta

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The general value of Log zeta is log of the modulus of zeta plus i times the general amplitude, where k is any integer fixed by the path.

symbols.meaning: general amplitude of zeta (2k pi + phi)
integer determined by the path of integration (winding number)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The general logarithm of a product equals the sum of the general logarithms; every value of each side is a value of the other, so the equation is completely true.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The principal-value form of the logarithm of a product is not true in all circumstances; the book gives z1 = z2 = (-1 + i sqrt 3)/2 as a counterexample.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For integer m, the general logarithm of z to the m equals m times the general logarithm of z; this is not completely true, since only one direction holds for all values.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The general logarithm of the reciprocal of z is minus the general logarithm of z; this equation is completely true.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The general logarithm of e to the zeta has values (1 + 2m pi i) zeta + 2n pi i, for integers m and n.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: exponential function
equations.statement: z is defined as the exponential of zeta when some value of Log z equals zeta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: When zeta is real, the complex exponential exp zeta equals the real exponential e to the zeta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The exponential of xi plus i eta has modulus e to the xi and amplitude eta.

symbols.meaning: imaginary part of zeta (amplitude of the result)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: functional relation of the exponential
equations.statement: The exponential function satisfies the functional relation f(zeta1 + zeta2) = f(zeta1) f(zeta2) for complex arguments.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For positive a and real zeta, the general power a to the zeta equals e to the zeta log a, the definition used in the earlier chapter.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The general power a to the zeta is defined as exp of zeta times any value of the logarithm of a, for any nonzero complex a and zeta.

symbols.meaning: any value of the logarithm of a

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The modulus of a general power a to the zeta depends on the integer m unless eta is zero, so the general power has infinitely many values.

symbols.meaning: integer labelling the branch of Log a

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The general value of e to the zeta, with integer m, is given in terms of xi and eta; its principal value is exp zeta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: On the second definition the logarithm to base e of z is doubly infinitely many-valued, given by this formula for integers m and n.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The product of a to the zeta and b to the zeta equals (ab) to the zeta; this is completely true but not always true of principal values.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The product of a to the zeta and a to the zeta-prime equals a to the zeta plus zeta-prime; this is not completely true but holds for principal values.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The function f of the real variable x equals p for positive x and q for negative x, since Im(log x) is 0 or pi.

symbols.meaning: function of the real variable x
constant value of f for positive x
constant value of f for negative x

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The exponential of a complex sum equals e^xi times (cos eta + i sin eta).

symbols.meaning: real part of the complex argument
imaginary part of the complex argument

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: Euler's formula
equations.statement: The exponential of i times eta equals cos eta plus i sin eta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Cosine of a real angle written as the average of exp(i eta) and exp(-i eta).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Sine of a real angle written in terms of exp(i eta) and exp(-i eta).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Defines cos zeta for every complex zeta by this exponential expression; it agrees with the elementary cosine for real zeta.

symbols.meaning: argument of the trigonometrical function, real or complex

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Defines sin zeta for every complex zeta by this exponential expression; it agrees with the elementary sine for real zeta.

symbols.meaning: argument of the trigonometrical function, real or complex

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Tangent defined as sine over cosine, for complex argument.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Cotangent defined as cosine over sine, for complex argument.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Secant defined as the reciprocal of cosine.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Cosecant defined as the reciprocal of sine.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Cosine written in terms of t = exp(i zeta).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Sine written in terms of t = exp(i zeta).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The sum of the squares of cosine and sine is 1 for all complex zeta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Sine of a sum of two complex arguments, in the same form as elementary trigonometry.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Shifting the argument by a right angle turns cosine into minus sine.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Shifting the argument by a right angle turns sine into cosine.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Defines the hyperbolic cosine for all complex zeta by this exponential expression.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Defines the hyperbolic sine for all complex zeta by this exponential expression.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Cosine of i zeta equals the hyperbolic cosine of zeta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Sine of i zeta equals i times the hyperbolic sine of zeta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Double-argument identity for the hyperbolic cosine, obtained by transforming the cosine double-angle formula.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Solutions of cos zeta = a for real a with -1 <= a <= 1 (real branch).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Integral of 1/(x^2 + alpha) for alpha > 0 is an inverse tangent.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Integral of 1/(x^2 + alpha) for alpha < 0 is a logarithm.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The formula the book proposes by analogy (i alpha written for alpha), with C a constant; the book then tests whether it holds.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Standard connection between the inverse tangent and the principal logarithm, true for real x; checked by putting x = tan y.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The exponential function equals its power series for all complex z.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The series sum F satisfies the functional equation of the exponential.

symbols.meaning: sum of the exponential power series

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Differential equation satisfied by f(y) = F(iy): its derivative is i times f.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: f(y) has modulus 1 and so can be written as cos Y + i sin Y for some angle function Y.

symbols.meaning: real angle, a function of y, with -pi < Y <= pi

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The exponential series at a pure imaginary argument gives cos y + i sin y for all real y.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.latex: F(x + iy) = F(x) F(iy) = \exp x(\cos y + i\sin y) = \exp(x + iy)
equations.statement: The exponential of a complex number x + iy is exp x times (cos y + i sin y).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Power series of cosine, valid for all complex z.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Power series of sine, valid for all complex z.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The principal logarithm of 1 + z equals its logarithmic series for |z| <= 1 except z = -1.

symbols.meaning: complex number with |z| <= 1, z not equal to -1

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Logarithmic series obtained by replacing z with -z in the previous series.

symbols.meaning: complex number, |z| <= 1, z not equal to 1

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The principal logarithm of 1 + z as an integral over the straight line C from 1 to 1 + z.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Power series of the inverse tangent for |z| < 1, obtained from the logarithmic series.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Sum of the cosine series for log(1 + e^(i theta)) on the unit circle, valid for theta not an odd multiple of pi.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Sum of the sine series for -pi < theta < pi; the sum is a periodic, discontinuous function of theta.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: logarithmic series
equations.statement: For |hz| < 1, the logarithm of 1 + hz is given by its power series in hz.

symbols.meaning: a real number small enough that |hz| < 1

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The quotient log(1 + hz)/h equals z plus a remainder term phi(h, z) that tends to zero as h tends to zero.

symbols.meaning: a real number small enough that |hz| < 1

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The limit as h tends to zero of log(1 + hz) divided by h is z.

symbols.meaning: a real number tending to zero

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Taking h = 1/n, n times the logarithm of (1 + z/n) tends to z as n tends to infinity.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: exponential limit
equations.statement: The limit of (1 + z/n) to the power n as n tends to infinity is the exponential exp z, a generalisation of the real case.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The derivative with respect to t of log(1 + tz) is z divided by 1 + tz.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For a complex function phi = psi + i chi of a real variable, the derivative of exp(phi) has the same form as for real phi: phi' exp(phi).

symbols.meaning: complex function of t, psi + i chi

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The nth derivative of (1 + tz)^m with respect to t is m(m-1)...(m-n+1) z^n (1 + tz)^(m-n).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The nth derivative at t = 0, divided by n factorial, gives the binomial coefficient times z^n. (The book writes phi^n(0) for the nth derivative.)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: Taylor's theorem with remainder
equations.statement: The value of phi at 1 equals its Taylor polynomial of degree n - 1 at 0 plus a remainder R_n.

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The remainder R_n is given by an integral of the nth derivative against (1 - t)^(n-1).

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: For z = r(cos theta + i sin theta) and 0 <= t <= 1, the modulus |1 + tz| is at least 1 - tr.

symbols.meaning: complex variable z = r(cos theta + i sin theta)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.name: binomial theorem (general form)
equations.statement: For all real m and real z between -1 and 1, (1 + z)^m equals exp of m times log(1 + z); the general form extends this to complex m and z with |z| < 1, using the principal value of the logarithm.

symbols.meaning: real or complex number, |z| < 1 in the general theorem

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: The ratio of successive absolute coefficients of the binomial series tends to 1, whether m is real or complex, so the series converges for |z| < 1.

symbols.meaning: coefficient of z^n in the binomial series, binom(m, n)

equations.location: THE GENERAL THEORY OF THE LOGARITHMIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS
equations.statement: Restated for the binomial series argument: derivative of (1 + tz)^m with respect to real t equals m z (1 + tz)^(m-1), each side with its principal value.

equations.location: The Proof that every Equation has a Root
equations.statement: The polynomial Z = P(z) is a sum of powers of z with constant coefficients, the highest power being z^n.

symbols.meaning: value of the polynomial P(z), a point in the Z-plane
independent complex variable, a point in the z-plane
coefficient of the power z^{n-k} in the polynomial, real or complex

equations.location: The Proof that every Equation has a Root
equations.statement: The modulus of Z is the modulus of the polynomial evaluated at x + iy, and it is a positive continuous function of x and y.

symbols.meaning: modulus of the complex number Z

equations.location: The Proof that every Equation has a Root
equations.statement: The point x_0 + i y_0 is a root of the polynomial P, so P has a root in the complex plane.

symbols.meaning: the polynomial in z with complex coefficients
real part of the point where the minimum of |P| is attained (the root)

equations.location: The Proof that every Equation has a Root
equations.statement: Near the point x_0 + i y_0, the value of P stays within half of rho of its value at that point, by continuity of P.

symbols.meaning: modulus |a| of the nonzero value a = P(x_0 + iy_0) in the contradiction argument
the assumed nonzero value P(x_0 + iy_0)

equations.location: The Proof that every Equation has a Root
equations.statement: Near x_0 + i y_0, P(x + iy) equals the constant a plus a small correction phi.

symbols.meaning: small correction term with |phi| < rho/2 inside the square

equations.location: The Proof that every Equation has a Root
equations.statement: One admissible choice of the decreasing sequence of side lengths delta_m is halving at each step.

symbols.meaning: side length of the m-th auxiliary square, decreasing to zero

problems.problem_latex:
A more general proposition, which is due to Gauss and includes those
which precede as particular cases, is the following: \emph{an algebraical equation
\[
x^{n} + p_{1}x^{n-1} + p_{2}x^{n-2} + \dots + p_{n} = 0,
\]
with integral coefficients, cannot have a rational but non-integral root}.

[For suppose that the equation has a root~$a/b$, where $a$~and~$b$ are integers
\PageSep{7}
without a common factor, and $b$~is positive. Writing~$a/b$ for~$x$, and multiplying
by~$b^{n-1}$, we obtain
\[
-\frac{a^{n}}{b} = p_{1}a^{n-1} + p_{2}a^{n-2}b + \dots + p_{n}b^{n-1},
\]
a fraction in its lowest terms equal to an integer, which is absurd. Thus $b = 1$,
and the root is~$a$. It is evident that $a$~must be a divisor of~$p_{n}$.]
problems.markdown: A more general proposition, which is due to Gauss and includes those which precede as particular cases, is the following: *an algebraical equation x^n + p_1x^n-1 + p_2x^n-2 + …+ p_n = 0, with integral coefficients, cannot have a rational but non-integral root*. [For suppose that the equation has a root $a/b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers [pg]7 without a common factor, and $b$ is positive. Writing $a/b$ for $x$, and multiplying by $b^{n-1}$, we obtain -a^nb = p_1a^n-1 + p_2a^n-2b + …+ p_nb^n-1, a fraction in its lowest terms equal to an integer, which is absurd. Thus $b = 1$, and the root is $a$. It is evident that $a$ must be a divisor of $p_{n}$.]

problems.problem_latex:
Show that the integral of $1/(a + b\cos x)$, where $a + b$~is positive, may
be expressed in one or other of the forms
\[
\frac{2}{\sqrtp{a^{2} - b^{2}}}
  \arctan \left\{t\bigsqrtp{\frac{a - b}{a + b}}\right\},\quad
\frac{1}{\sqrtp{b^{2} - a^{2}}}
  \log \left|\frac{\sqrtp{b + a} + t\sqrtp{b - a}}
                  {\sqrtp{b + a} - t\sqrtp{b - a}}\right|,
\]
where $t = \tan\frac{1}{2}x$, according as $a^{2} > b^{2}$ or $a^{2} < b^{2}$. If $a^{2} = b^{2}$ then the integral
reduces to a constant multiple of that of $\sec^{2}\frac{1}{2}x$ or $\cosec^{2}\frac{1}{2}x$, and its value
may at once be written down. Deduce the forms of the integral when $a + b$
is negative.

problems.problem_latex:
\Topic{Polar coordinates.} Show that the area bounded by the curve
$r = f(\theta)$, where $f(\theta)$~is a one-valued function of~$\theta$, and the radii $\theta = \theta_{1}$, $\theta = \theta_{2}$, is
$F(\theta_{2}) - F(\theta_{1})$, where $\ds F(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2} \int r^{2}\, d\theta$. And the length of the corresponding
arc of the curve is $\Phi(\theta_{2}) - \Phi(\theta_{1})$, where
\[
\Phi(\theta)
  = \bigint \bigsqrtb{r^{2} + \biggl(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\biggr)^{2}}\, d\theta.
\]

Hence determine (i)~the area and perimeter of the circle $r = 2a\sin\theta$;
(ii)~the area between the parabola $r = \frac{1}{2}l\sec^{2} \frac{1}{2}\theta$ and its latus rectum, and the
length of the corresponding arc of the parabola; (iii)~the area of the limaçon
$r = a + b\cos\theta$, distinguishing the cases in which $a > b$, $a = b$, and $a < b$;
and (iv)~the areas of the ellipses $1/r^{2} = a\cos^{2} \theta + 2h\cos\theta\sin\theta + b\sin^{2} \theta$ and
$l/r = 1 + e\cos\theta$. [In the last case we are led to the integral $\ds \int \frac{d\theta}{(1 + e\cos\theta)^{2}}$,
which may be calculated (cf.\ \Ex{liii}.~4) by the help of the substitution
\[
(1 + e\cos\theta) (1 - e\cos\phi) = 1 - e^{2}.]
\]
